South Africa has demarched Nigeria’s High Commissioner to the country, Femi Fani-Kayode, over the controversy surrounding the presentation of his letters of credence and his subsequent remarks on social media. The South African Broadcasting Corporation reported the development on Tuesday, citing a statement by the country’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation. According to the statement, DIRCO Director-General, Zane Dangor, had earlier met with Fani-Kayode to formally convey South Africa’s concerns over events following the presentation of his diplomatic credentials to President Cyril Ramaphosa. “During the meeting, the Director-General conveyed South Africa’s concern regarding events that transpired following the presentation of the High Commissioner’s Letters of Credence to His Excellency President Cyril Ramaphosa, as well as subsequent remarks made on social media,” the statement read. Dangor reaffirmed the importance of preserving the longstanding bilateral relationship between Nigeria and South Africa, which he said was founded on mutual respect, friendship and cooperation. He also drew Fani-Kayode’s attention to Article 41 of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which requires diplomatic agents to conduct official business with the receiving country through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs. South Africa, however, reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening its strategic partnership with Nigeria and maintaining constructive diplomatic engagement based on African solidarity and mutual respect. The diplomatic development follows a controversy that erupted after Fani-Kayode presented his letters of credence to Ramaphosa at the Presidential Guest House in Pretoria on Friday, alongside ambassadors from 14 other countries. The former Minister of Aviation had alleged that the South African Presidency deliberately excluded his introduction and speech from the livestream of the ceremony, insisting that the addresses of the other diplomats were broadcast. In a post on his X handle after the event, Fani-Kayode said, “Every single one of the 15 Ambassadors that were present were introduced formally and gave a speech. Curiously the South African Presidency refused to air the introduction of my goodself and the Nigerian delegation or to air my speech. “They went a step further by cutting us out of the livestream completely and went back on livestream only after my speech was concluded.” He also claimed that he raised the matter with Ramaphosa during a photo session after the ceremony, adding that the South African President directed relevant officials to address his complaint. Fani-Kayode subsequently declined an interview request from the South African Broadcasting Corporation, saying he was dissatisfied with the treatment of the Nigerian delegation. However, Ramaphosa’s spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya, disputed the envoy’s account, saying the President did not intervene in the operations of the public broadcaster. Magwenya said Ramaphosa had merely referred Fani-Kayode to Sophie Mokoena, the SABC’s acting political and foreign editor, as the appropriate person to address his complaint. “The SABC is a public broadcaster. The President carries no legal or political mandate to interfere with its operations or intervene in its editorial processes,” Magwenya said. He described Fani-Kayode’s handling of the complaint as “grossly inappropriate”, arguing that the envoy had misunderstood what he called a minor operational issue. The South African Presidency subsequently released a separate video of Fani-Kayode’s speech on its YouTube channel, hours after the envoy protested its omission from the initial livestream. The disagreement also triggered an exchange between the Nigerian High Commission and Magwenya, with the mission defending Fani-Kayode and insisting that Ramaphosa intervened to resolve the matter. The latest meeting between Dangor and Fani-Kayode marks a formal diplomatic response to the controversy, with South Africa stressing the need for official communications to follow established channels.
